1: Between September 1960 and January 1961 a woman came to a street in a poor quarter on the eastern side of Rome roughly once a week, always after dark, always alone, and always on foot for the last three hundred metres. Fourteen people saw her over those four months. Not one of them saw more than about ninety seconds of any visit. This story is made out of those fourteen fragments, and the reason to tell it that way is that every one of them was wrong. Not slightly wrong in the way witnesses usually are, about the colour of a coat or the hour. Wrong about the entire nature of what they were looking at, all fourteen, for four months, and several stayed wrong for thirty years afterward. The street was called Via dei Cappellari, which is not its real name, and it had eleven buildings on it and a shop at the corner and a man who mended shoes in a room the size of a wardrobe, and the thing you need to understand about a street like that in 1960 is that nothing happened on it that was not immediately known to everybody. There was no privacy available and nobody expected any. A street like that is not nosy in the disapproving sense of the word; it is a system for keeping track of who is all right and who is not, and it runs on exactly the kind of information a stranger arriving after dark generates. So when a woman in an expensive but very plain coat began arriving on Thursday evenings and going into number seven and coming out fifty or sixty minutes later, it was not a private matter and was never going to be. It took about three weeks for the street to work out who she was. It took a further thirty-eight years for anybody on it to find out what she had been doing there, and by then eleven of the fourteen were dead.
2: Take the first two, because between them they set the shape of everything the street believed afterward. Signora Bruni ran the shop on the corner and saw her four times, always through glass, always at an angle, and gave a description in 1998 that was accurate about the coat and the shoes and wrong about the height by eight centimetres. What she noticed, and repeated for the rest of her life, was that the woman never bought anything and never looked in, and she had spent twenty years behind that counter learning that people who do not look in do not want to be spoken to. From that single observation, which was correct, she built a conclusion, which was not: that the woman was ashamed. It is worth stopping on that, because it is the engine of everything that followed. Signora Bruni was intelligent and fair and was reasoning properly from good evidence. The step she took without noticing she had taken it, and that thirteen other people took after her, was from does not want to be seen to has a reason to hide, and there is no logic that gets you from the first to the second. Then there was Nardo, who mended shoes, and who was the only one of the fourteen who ever spoke to her. He said good evening on a Thursday in October and she said good evening back and asked him whether the rain was going to hold off, and he said it was not, and she thanked him and went in. Eleven words. He thought about those eleven words a great deal over the following four months, because of the one thing about them that did not fit, which was that she had asked it the way you ask a question whose answer you actually want, and people doing something shameful, in Nardo's considerable experience, do not stop to ask about the weather.
3: By the end of October the street had three theories and had begun to argue about them. The first, belonging mostly to the women on the lower floors, was that there was a married man in number seven, and it had the advantage of explaining the hour and the discretion and the walking, and the disadvantage of being contradicted by the fact that everybody in number seven was known and none of them fitted. The second, favoured by two of the older men, was money: that she was paying something off, that the plain coat was a deliberate reduction, and that the whole thing was a transaction of a kind not considered remarkable in that quarter at all. That one lost its adherents in November, when somebody pointed out that the parcel went up full and did not come down, which is not how a debt works. The third was medical, and it was closest to right and still completely wrong. It held that somebody in the building was ill and that she was a relative, and it collapsed because the street knew who was ill in number seven and knew she had no relatives living. What none of the three could accommodate, and what was discussed a great deal and never resolved, was the walking. She could have been driven to the door. She was not. She got out three streets away every time, in December weather that was genuinely unpleasant, and walked the rest, and no theory anybody had explained why a woman would do that. The answer, when it came thirty-eight years later, was so plain that two of the three surviving witnesses refused at first to accept it: a car at that door would have been discussed, and being discussed was the one thing she was preventing, so she walked. The street had built elaborate structures on top of a woman's decision to get out early.
4: The person who saw the most was a boy of nine called Tonino who lived on the second floor of number seven and understood the least, which is usually how it goes. He passed her on the stairs eleven times. He was not curious about her the way the adults were, because he was nine and she was a woman who came on Thursdays, so the things he remembered were the things nobody else thought to record. That she always carried the same brown paper parcel, the size of a shoebox, going up, and never coming down. That she took the stairs slowly and stopped on the third landing every time, not out of breath, just stopping. That she said good evening to him every time in the same two words in the same order, and that he had found this funny by about the fifth time and started saying them back the same flat way, and that she had noticed and never let on. That her shoes were quiet, which he mentioned because nobody else's on those stairs were. That once, in December, she was crying on the way down and did it in a way he did not recognise as crying until he was about thirty, because her face was doing nothing at all and she said good evening on the way past in the usual voice. And one more thing, mentioned in 1998 almost as an afterthought, which turned out to be the key to the whole business: that from the landing, on Thursdays, you could hear a piano. Not somebody playing a piece. The same four bars, over and over, stopping and starting, sometimes for the better part of an hour. He had assumed for thirty-eight years that it was somebody learning. It was the exact opposite. It was somebody who had known the piece for forty years arriving each week at the place where her hands stopped knowing it, and going back, and arriving there again.
5: Here is what was actually happening in the room, which nobody on that street learned until 1998 and which can be told in four sentences. In 1947 a woman called Elsa Vermeer taught ballet in a first-floor room in Amsterdam to a class of eleven girls, one of whom was Audrey, for four months and no longer, because the class ran out of money. Thirteen years later Elsa was sixty-eight, living alone in Rome in one room in number seven, and had been going blind for six years and was by 1960 almost entirely without sight. She had no children and one nephew in Antwerp who wrote at Christmas. She could not read, could not teach, and could no longer play the piano she had used for classes for forty years, except four bars of a Chopin waltz her hands still knew and that she worked at every week without ever reaching the fifth. The parcel was food, and it was food chosen by somebody who had thought about it: things that did not need to be seen to be eaten, and nothing that had to be cut up. The fifty minutes was reading aloud, mostly newspapers, sometimes letters Elsa had received and could not read, occasionally a novel that took them eight months and that they never finished and both of them, by the end, were pretending to like more than they did. The rent on the room had been paid since March 1960 by a bank in Zurich through an arrangement Elsa had been told was a pension from a teachers' association that did not exist. That is the whole of it. There is no scandal in it anywhere and that is exactly why it was invisible to a street that had spent four months looking for one. Fourteen people held a great deal of accurate information and were searching it for the wrong thing, which has nothing to do with how clever any of them were.
6: So the question is why she did not simply say. She was not, in 1960, a woman who found it difficult to be seen doing a decent thing; she did decent things in public constantly and was perfectly comfortable with it. The reason was Elsa, and it was specific, and she explained it once. Elsa did not know who she was. She knew the voice, and she knew the visitor was one of the eleven girls from 1947, and had decided at some point that it was the tall one who had been quite good and had gone into an office somewhere, and Audrey had let her believe it and gone on letting her believe it for sixteen months. She had answered to it. When Elsa said something that only made sense if the visitor were the tall one, she agreed, and twice she invented a small detail to hold it together. This was not a kindness she was proud of. She said afterward that she had told herself at first that correcting it would upset an old woman for no reason, and that this had been true for about the first three visits and self-serving for all the rest. Because what she actually could not face was the specific silence that would follow. Elsa had never in her life accepted a thing she had not earned, and the moment she understood that her Thursday visitor was famous and rich, the reading would become charity and the food would become charity and Elsa would say thank you politely and the whole thing would be finished inside a month. It was the only room in her life where she was nobody in particular, where nothing she said was going to be repeated and nothing she did was going to be counted to her credit, and she had not had one of those since she was about twenty-two. She was terrified of losing it, and she lost it anyway, in a way she had not planned for.
7: Elsa died on the eleventh of February 1963, of something entirely unrelated to her eyes, in the room, in the afternoon, with nobody there. The street found out on the twelfth and behaved the way that street behaved, which is to say that four women who had spent two years discussing the woman in the plain coat, and who between them had constructed most of the theory about the married man, went up and cleaned the room and laid the old teacher out properly and did it well. Both things were true about them at once and neither cancels the other. The funeral was on the fifteenth and nineteen people came, and the woman in the plain coat was not among them, and the street noticed that and drew from it the conclusion you would expect, and it was the last and cruellest of the fourteen wrong readings. She was in Switzerland and did not know. Nobody had her address; Elsa had never had it; the arrangement with the bank ran one way only and had no instruction in it for this. She found out eight days later, from a letter written by Nardo the shoemaker, who had worked out on his own that the visitor would want to be told, and who did not know where to send it either and had sent it to a film company in Rome with her name on the envelope and no other information, and it took eight days and four pairs of hands and it arrived. The letter was six lines long and said where and when and that it had been peaceful and that the room had been seen to, and it did not ask her for anything and did not mention that he had spent two and a half years wondering who she was. She wrote back to him. That letter, and the fact that a shoemaker kept it in a tin for thirty-five years, is the reason any of this is known at all.
8: She came to the street once more, in April 1963, in daylight, and knocked on Nardo's door and sat in the room the size of a wardrobe for about two hours. He asked her, directly, at the end of it, what she had been doing in number seven, because he had waited two and a half years to ask and had decided he was owed it, and she told him, all of it, including the part about the tall one who had gone into an office. He said the part that had stayed with him was that she told it badly, in the wrong order, going back to add things, like somebody who had never said any of it out loud before, which he thought afterward she probably had not. Then she asked him not to tell anybody, and he said he would not, and he did not, for thirty-five years, through the deaths of eleven of the other thirteen and through at least a dozen conversations in which the old theory about the married man was repeated in front of him. He told it in 1998, at ninety-one, six weeks before he died, to his granddaughter, who was writing something for a local history society and had asked him an entirely different question. He said that he had kept it because he had been asked to and that he was telling it now because everybody it could embarrass was dead, and then he said the thing that has survived best out of the whole business, which was that the street had watched a woman for four months and had between them produced fourteen accounts and three theories and not one person had considered the possibility that she was simply reading a newspaper to somebody. This story is a work of fiction. Elsa, Nardo, Tonino, the street and every detail in it are invented, created for storytelling and not drawn from any record.
